MSK / Week 14 / Pectoral Region and Axilla
Question 1827
During a dissection of the upper limb, the brachial fascia is incised and the muscles lying posterior to the humerus are reflected as a single group. The muscles in this space share one functional role at the elbow. Which of the following best describes the muscle group found in this compartment?
A. Rotator muscles
B. Flexor muscles
C. Abductor muscles
D. Extensor muscles
E. Adductor muscles
Answer: D. Extensor muscles
Order: First
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Regions and fascial compartments of the upper limb
Why this is correct:
The lecture divides both the arm and the forearm into an anterior compartment holding flexor muscles and a posterior compartment holding extensor muscles, so muscles posterior to the humerus are extensors.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. The lecture doesn't describe a rotator compartment in the arm.
B. Flexors occupy the anterior compartment of the arm, not the posterior one.
C. The lecture doesn't describe an abductor compartment in the arm.
E. The lecture doesn't describe an adductor compartment in the arm.
Objective: Identify the muscles of the pectoral region. Discuss their attachments, innervation, and actions. Describe the clinical implications of nerve damage and their loss of function.

C. The lecture doesn't place the sternal angle at T2/T3.

Reference: Mastectomy and breast reconstruction
Why this is correct:
The lecture defines a total or simple mastectomy as removal of all breast tissue including the nipple, the areola, and most of the overlying skin, while leaving the pectoral muscles beneath.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. A radical mastectomy removes the axillary nodes and the pectoral muscles as well.
C. Sentinel node biopsy samples a node rather than removing the breast.
D. Axillary dissection removes nodes from the axilla rather than the breast itself.
E. A modified radical mastectomy also removes some axillary lymph nodes, which weren't taken here.
Objective: Discuss the anatomical basis for the following conditions associated with breast cancer: dimpling of skin, nipple retraction, peau d'orange sign, lymphogenous metastasis (pathways for spread), sentinel lymph node biopsy, lymphedema in the upper extremity, and reconstructive options following mastectomy.

The apex of the axilla is the small triangular gap between the clavicle, the first rib, and the superior border of the scapula, and it forms the cervico-axillary canal between the neck and the axilla.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. The manubrium and acromion are not listed as boundaries of the apex.
C. The humeral head lies at the lateral wall, not at the apex.
D. The scapular spine and second rib are not listed as boundaries of the apex.
E. The second rib and coracoid process are not listed as boundaries of the apex.
Objective: Discuss the contents and boundaries of the axilla.

MSK / Week 14 / Pectoral Region and Axilla
Question 1896
A 29-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a stab wound to the armpit. He has a cool, pulseless upper limb, a rapidly expanding hematoma, and weakness in several muscle groups of the arm and forearm. Which of the following groups of structures is most likely injured together?
A. Axillary artery, axillary vein, and cords of the brachial plexus
B. Subclavian artery, internal jugular vein, and cervical plexus
C. Internal thoracic artery, azygos vein, and intercostal nerves
D. Lateral thoracic artery, thoracic duct, and phrenic nerve
E. Brachial artery, cephalic vein, and roots of the brachial plexus
Answer: A. Axillary artery, axillary vein, and cords of the brachial plexus
Order: Second
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Contents of the axilla
Why this is correct:
The contents of the axilla are the axillary artery and its branches, the axillary vein and its tributaries, the cords and branches of the brachial plexus, the axillary lymph nodes, and axillary fat, so a single penetrating wound can injure all three together.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. These structures lie in the neck rather than in the axilla.
C. These structures lie within the thorax.
D. The thoracic duct and phrenic nerve are not axillary contents.
E. The brachial artery and the plexus roots lie distal and proximal to the axilla respectively.
Objective: Discuss the contents and boundaries of the axilla.

D. Brachial vein

Answer: A. Axillary vein

Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Cephalic vein and the deltopectoral groove; Axillary vein and the axillary sheath
Why this is correct:

Why the other answers are wrong:

E. The subclavian vein begins only after the axillary vein crosses the lateral border of the first rib.
Objective: Identify and discuss the venous drainage patterns of the axillary and cephalic veins.

Question 1953
During a cadaver dissection of the upper limb, the tendon of the long head of the biceps brachii is traced proximally out of the arm and is found lying within a bony groove on the anterior aspect of the proximal humerus. Which of the following bony features is most likely holding the tendon at this point?

B. Radial groove
C. Intertubercular sulcus
D. Coronoid fossa
E. Surgical neck
Answer: C. Intertubercular sulcus
Order: Second
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Proximal humerus landmarks of the arm; Biceps brachii
Why this is correct:
The intertubercular sulcus, also called the bicipital groove, is the groove on the anterior aspect of the proximal humerus, and the lecture identifies it as the groove occupied by the tendon of the long head of the biceps brachii.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. The anatomical neck is the constriction next to the head and isn't a groove for a tendon.
B. The radial groove lies on the posterior aspect of the humeral shaft, not on the anterior proximal humerus.
D. The coronoid fossa is a depression at the distal end of the humerus.
E. The surgical neck is the narrowed region distal to the tubercles, not a tendon groove.
Objective: Identify the bony features, articulations, and associated ligaments of the humerus, proximal radius, and ulna. Discuss the anatomical and clinical considerations of fractures of these bones and radial head subluxation.

A 26-year-old man sustains a deep laceration to the back of the arm. He subsequently has weakness of extension of the forearm and of the wrist and fingers, while elbow flexion and supination are intact. Which of the following nerves is most likely injured?
A. Ulnar nerve
B. Radial nerve
C. Musculocutaneous nerve
D. Lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm
E. Median nerve
Answer: B. Radial nerve
Order: Third
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Radial nerve in the arm; Neurovasculature of the posterior compartment of the arm
Why this is correct:
The radial nerve enters the posterior compartment of the arm and supplies all of the muscles of the posterior compartment of both the arm and the forearm, so a posterior arm injury produces weak extension while the anterior compartment functions are spared.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. The ulnar nerve passes through the anterior compartment and gives no branches in the arm.
C. A musculocutaneous injury would weaken elbow flexion and supination instead.
D. That nerve is sensory and wouldn't produce weakness.
E. The median nerve travels with the brachial artery in the anterior compartment and gives no branches in the arm.
Objective: Describe the course and targets (i.e., muscular and cutaneous innervation) of the musculocutaneous, median, and ulnar nerves within the arm. Describe common sites of injury to neural structures and subsequent clinical manifestations. Describe the bicipital myotatic reflex.

Question 2013
A patient holds the elbow in full flexion for a prolonged period, which narrows the brachial artery where it crosses the front of the joint, yet the forearm stays well perfused throughout. Which of the following best explains this finding?
A. The profunda brachii artery enlarges to replace the radial and ulnar arteries
B. The superficial veins of the arm take over arterial supply to the forearm
C. The brachial veins reverse their flow to supply the forearm tissues
D. A network of arteries around the elbow carries blood past the narrowed segment
E. The bicipital aponeurosis protects the artery from any narrowing in flexion
Answer: D. A network of arteries around the elbow carries blood past the narrowed segment
Order: Third
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Elbow anastomosis and collateral circulation
Why this is correct:
The lecture describes the elbow anastomosis as a network of arteries surrounding the elbow joint that ensures continuous perfusion regardless of the position of the joint or if a main artery is compressed or blocked.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. The lecture doesn't describe the profunda brachii replacing the terminal branches.
B. Superficial veins drain the limb rather than perfuse it.
C. Veins return blood toward the heart and don't supply tissue with arterial blood.
E. The bicipital aponeurosis forms part of the roof of the cubital fossa and isn't described as protecting against narrowing.
Objective: Trace the courses of the major arteries, superficial and deep veins, and lymphatics within the arm. Define collateral circulation and describe why it is important at joints in general and specifically at the elbow. Identify sites where a pulse rate can be measured.

Question 2014
A student preparing a summary of the blood supply of the arm is asked which vessels contribute to the arterial network surrounding the elbow joint, the network that keeps the forearm perfused when the main vessel is compressed. A. Cephalic, basilic, median cubital, and brachial vessels
B. Profunda brachii, axillary, subclavian, and brachial arteries
C. Superior ulnar collateral, inferior ulnar collateral, radial, and ulnar arteries
D. Radial collateral, middle collateral, superior ulnar collateral, and inferior ulnar collateral arteries

Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Elbow anastomosis and collateral circulation; Brachial artery

The lecture's collateral vessels of the arm are the radial and middle collateral branches of the profunda brachii plus the superior and inferior ulnar collateral branches of the brachial artery, and these form the network around the elbow joint.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. These are veins, which don't form an arterial anastomosis.
B. The axillary and subclavian arteries lie far proximal to the elbow.
C. The radial and ulnar arteries are the terminal branches the collaterals rejoin rather than collaterals themselves.
E. These are the main trunks of the limb rather than the collateral vessels that bypass the joint.
Objective: Trace the courses of the major arteries, superficial and deep veins, and lymphatics within the arm. Define collateral circulation and describe why it is important at joints in general and specifically at the elbow. Identify sites where a pulse rate can be measured.

Question 2024
A student begins a dissection of the front of the elbow by incising the layer that covers the cubital fossa from the surface, and notes while cutting that this layer is continuous above with the deep fascia of the arm and below with the deep fascia of the forearm. Which of the following best describes the layer being divided?
A. The tendon of the biceps brachii and the brachialis muscle
B. The lateral intermuscular septum together with the brachial fascia
C. Brachial fascia alone, without any tendinous reinforcement
D. The medial intermuscular septum together with the antebrachial fascia
E. Brachial and antebrachial fascia reinforced by the bicipital aponeurosis
Answer: E. Brachial and antebrachial fascia reinforced by the bicipital aponeurosis
Order: Second
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Boundaries of the cubital fossa; Biceps brachii
Why this is correct:
The lecture gives the superficial boundary, or roof, of the cubital fossa as the brachial and antebrachial fascia together with the bicipital aponeurosis.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. The biceps tendon is a content of the fossa and the brachialis is part of its floor.
B. The lateral intermuscular septum lies in the arm and doesn't roof the fossa.
C. The lecture includes the bicipital aponeurosis in the roof, so the fascia isn't acting alone.
D. The medial intermuscular septum is also a structure of the arm.
Objective: Describe the boundaries, contents, and relationships of structures found in the cubital fossa.

MSK / Week 14 / Anterior Arm and Cubital Fossa
Question 2025
A student is asked to list the three main contents of the cubital fossa in the order in which a probe would meet them if it were moved across the fossa from the lateral side toward the medial side, using the three letter mnemonic given in the lecture. Which of the following sequences is most likely correct?
A. Median nerve, tendon of the biceps brachii, brachial artery
B. Tendon of the biceps brachii, median nerve, brachial artery
C. Median nerve, brachial artery, tendon of the biceps brachii
D. Tendon of the biceps brachii, brachial artery, median nerve
E. Brachial artery, median nerve, tendon of the biceps brachii
Answer: D. Tendon of the biceps brachii, brachial artery, median nerve
Order: First
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Contents of the cubital fossa
Why this is correct:
The lecture uses the mnemonic TAN for the contents of the cubital fossa from lateral to medial, standing for tendon of the biceps brachii muscle, brachial artery, and median nerve.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. The tendon is the most lateral of the three.
B. The median nerve is the most medial of the three, not the middle one.
C. This is the medial to lateral order, which reverses the mnemonic.
E. The brachial artery sits between the tendon and the nerve rather than most laterally.
Objective: Describe the boundaries, contents, and relationships of structures found in the cubital fossa.

MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm
Question 2028
The shoulder complex positions the hand for both gross and skilled tasks and at the same time carries load from the upper extremity into the trunk. Which of the following pairs of properties is most critical for the complex to achieve both of those roles?
A. Stability and ligamentous laxity
B. Stability and congruency
C. Mobility and stability
D. Mobility and ligamentous laxity
E. Mobility and congruency
Answer: C. Mobility and stability
Order: First
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Purpose of the shoulder complex
Why this is correct:
The lecture frames the shoulder complex around two requirements. It has to be mobile enough to place the hand almost anywhere in space, and stable enough to serve as a strong base while loads pass through it.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Ligamentous laxity isn't listed as a requirement, and stability alone doesn't supply mobility.
B. Stability alone with congruency would give a strong base but not the range the hand needs.
D. Ligamentous laxity isn't listed as a requirement of the complex.
E. Congruency isn't one of the two stated requirements, and the glenohumeral joint is deliberately incongruent.
Objective: Describe the anatomical characteristics (osteology, ligaments, tendons, and capsule) of the sternoclavicular, acromioclavicular and glenohumeral joints. Discuss the functions of the joints, and distinguish the nerves that convey joint pain and proprioception following Hilton's Law.

MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm
Question 2029
A 24-year-old man is lifting a loaded barbell overhead when his shoulder gives way. In working through the injury, the examiner considers how force generated in the upper extremity normally reaches the trunk. Which of the following best describes this function of the shoulder complex?
A. It absorbs loads within the upper extremity so the trunk stays unloaded
B. It distributes loads from the upper extremity into the cervical spine alone
C. It redirects loads from the upper extremity into the thoracic cage muscles
D. It transmits loads from the upper extremity to the axial skeleton
E. It transmits loads from the axial skeleton to the upper extremity
Answer: D. It transmits loads from the upper extremity to the axial skeleton
Order: Second
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Purpose of the shoulder complex
Why this is correct:
One of the two stated purposes of the shoulder complex is to transmit loads from the upper extremity to the axial skeleton, which is why the complex has to be strong as well as mobile.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. The complex transfers load rather than absorbing it so the trunk is spared.
B. The load reaches the axial skeleton as a whole, not the cervical spine alone.
C. The thoracic cage muscles aren't the destination named for this load transfer.
E. The direction is reversed, since the load being carried is generated in the limb.
Objective: Describe the anatomical characteristics (osteology, ligaments, tendons, and capsule) of the sternoclavicular, acromioclavicular and glenohumeral joints. Discuss the functions of the joints, and distinguish the nerves that convey joint pain and proprioception following Hilton's Law.

MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm
Question 2030
A 58-year-old woman has a stiff, painful shoulder after several weeks in a sling. Her grip strength and finger movements are normal, but she can't bring her hand to her mouth or reach behind her back. Which of the following functions of the shoulder complex has been most directly lost?
A. Providing the intrinsic force needed for the hand's pinch and grip
B. Providing a mobile base that positions the hand for its gross and skilled tasks
C. Providing the vascular supply needed for sustained activity of the hand
D. Providing the sensory feedback needed for the hand's skilled movements
E. Providing a rigid base that holds the hand in a single working position
Answer: B. Providing a mobile base that positions the hand for its gross and skilled tasks
Order: Second
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Purpose of the shoulder complex
Why this is correct:
The complex exists to give the hand a very mobile yet strong base so the hand can carry out its intricate gross and skilled functions. When the shoulder stiffens, the hand itself still works but can no longer be placed where it's needed.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Pinch and grip force comes from the hand and forearm, not from the shoulder complex.
C. Vascular supply to the hand isn't the function the complex is described as serving.
D. The complex is described in terms of mobility and stability, not sensory feedback for the hand.
E. A rigid base is the opposite of what the complex provides.
Objective: Describe the anatomical characteristics (osteology, ligaments, tendons, and capsule) of the sternoclavicular, acromioclavicular and glenohumeral joints. Discuss the functions of the joints, and distinguish the nerves that convey joint pain and proprioception following Hilton's Law.

MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm
Question 2031
During a physical examination of the shoulder, the clinician follows a subcutaneous bone with a fingertip from the midline of the sternum laterally to the point of the shoulder, feeling it along its whole length without losing contact. Which of the following structures is most likely being palpated?
A. Spine of the scapula
B. Acromion
C. Shaft of the humerus
D. Clavicle
E. Coracoid process
Answer: D. Clavicle
Order: First
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Clavicle in the shoulder complex
Why this is correct:
The clavicle runs from the manubrium to the acromion and is visible and palpable along its entire length, which is unusual for a bone of the shoulder.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. The spine of the scapula is palpable posteriorly and doesn't reach the sternum.
B. The acromion is a short lateral process and can't be followed to the midline.
C. The humeral shaft lies in the arm, distal to the point of the shoulder.
E. The coracoid process is a small hook on the anterior scapula, not a bone spanning to the sternum.
Objective: Identify the bony features of the clavicle, scapula, and humerus. Discuss common sites of fractures, predict what structures may be at risk, and discuss what sensory &/or motor deficits may occur.

Question 2032
A 19-year-old football player is examined after a blow to the shoulder, and the clinician palpates both ends of the clavicle in turn, checking each articulation for tenderness and step-off. Which of the following pairs of joints is being examined?
A. Sternoclavicular and glenohumeral
B. Sternoclavicular and acromioclavicular
C. Acromioclavicular and scapulothoracic
D. Acromioclavicular and glenohumeral
E. Sternoclavicular and scapulothoracic
Answer: B. Sternoclavicular and acromioclavicular
Order: Second
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Clavicle in the shoulder complex; Sternoclavicular joint: type and articulation
Why this is correct:
The medial end of the clavicle articulates with the manubrium at the sternoclavicular joint and the lateral end articulates with the acromion at the acromioclavicular joint, so palpating both ends examines both joints.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. The glenohumeral joint is between the humeral head and the glenoid fossa, not at an end of the clavicle.
C. Neither pairing is complete, since the scapulothoracic interface doesn't involve the clavicle directly.
D. Only one of these two involves the clavicle.
E. The scapulothoracic interface is the scapula moving on the thorax and has no clavicular end.
Objective: Identify the bony features of the clavicle, scapula, and humerus. Discuss common sites of fractures, predict what structures may be at risk, and discuss what sensory &/or motor deficits may occur.

MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm
Question 2033
A 7-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after falling onto his shoulder. Before any imaging is obtained, the clinician detects a clear step-off deformity in the bone simply by running a finger along it. Which of the following properties of this bone most directly allows that?
A. It's enclosed within the fibers of the pectoralis major
B. It's surrounded by a thick layer of subcutaneous fat
C. It's visible and palpable along its entire length
D. It lies deep to the trapezius along its medial half
E. It's covered by the deltoid along its lateral half
Answer: C. It's visible and palpable along its entire length
Order: Second
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Clavicle in the shoulder complex; Clavicle fracture
Why this is correct:
The clavicle is described as visible and palpable along its entire length, so a displaced fracture anywhere along it can usually be felt directly through the skin.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. The clavicle isn't enclosed within pectoralis major.
B. Overlying fat would blunt the contour rather than sharpen it.
D. Lying deep to a muscle would make palpation harder, not easier.
E. Muscle covering the bone would hide a step-off rather than reveal it.
Objective: Identify the bony features of the clavicle, scapula, and humerus. Discuss common sites of fractures, predict what structures may be at risk, and discuss what sensory &/or motor deficits may occur.

MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm
Question 2034
A 16-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after falling onto an outstretched hand during a soccer match. A radiograph shows a fractured clavicle, broken through the weakest part of the bone. Which of the following sites does the fracture most likely involve?
A. The inferior surface at the subclavian groove
B. The sternal end at the sternoclavicular joint
C. Junction of the middle and lateral thirds
D. The acromial end at the acromioclavicular joint
E. Junction of the medial and middle thirds
Answer: C. Junction of the middle and lateral thirds
Order: Second
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Clavicle fracture
Why this is correct:
The clavicle is commonly fractured from an indirect force transmitted through a fall on an outstretched hand or from a direct fall on the shoulder. The typed notes locate its weakest part at the junction of its middle and lateral thirds. The slide phrases the same point as most common at the middle third, so be ready for either wording.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. The subclavian groove is a surface marking, not the usual fracture site.
B. The sternoclavicular joint is strongly bound and usually survives when the bone fails.
D. The acromial end isn't named as the weakest part of the clavicle.
E. The medial end of the bone is thicker and isn't the described weak point.
Objective: Identify the bony features of the clavicle, scapula, and humerus. Discuss common sites of fractures, predict what structures may be at risk, and discuss what sensory &/or motor deficits may occur.

MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm
Question 2035
A 22-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after falling directly onto his shoulder. A radiograph confirms a fractured clavicle, and on inspection the affected shoulder sits visibly lower than the opposite side. Which of the following best explains the dropped shoulder?
A. Deltoid pulls the medial fragment down toward the thoracic wall
B. Sternocleidomastoid pulls the lateral fragment down toward the thorax
C. Trapezius can't hold the lateral fragment up against the weight of the limb
D. Subclavius depresses both fragments down against the first rib
E. Pectoralis major lifts the medial fragment above the lateral fragment
Answer: C. Trapezius can't hold the lateral fragment up against the weight of the limb
Order: Third
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Clavicle fracture; Clavicle in the shoulder complex
Why this is correct:
Once the clavicle is broken, the trapezius is unable to hold up the lateral fragment against the weight of the upper extremity, so the shoulder drops.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Deltoid attaches to the lateral third and the acromion, not the medial fragment.
B. Sternocleidomastoid acts on the medial fragment and elevates it rather than pulling the lateral fragment down.
D. Subclavius is small and isn't the reason the shoulder drops after a fracture.
E. Pectoralis major doesn't lift the medial fragment, and that wouldn't lower the shoulder.
Objective: Identify the bony features of the clavicle, scapula, and humerus. Discuss common sites of fractures, predict what structures may be at risk, and discuss what sensory &/or motor deficits may occur.

Question 2036
A 30-year-old woman sustains a clavicular fracture in a bicycle crash. On the radiograph the fragment closest to the midline is clearly displaced superiorly relative to the other fragment. Which of the following muscles most directly produces that displacement?
A. Pectoralis major
B. Subclavius

E. Sternocleidomastoid
Answer: E. Sternocleidomastoid
Order: Third
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Clavicle fracture

After a clavicular fracture the sternocleidomastoid elevates the medial fragment of bone, which is why the fragment nearer the midline rides superiorly.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Pectoralis major is one of the adductors that may pull the lateral fragment medially.
B. Subclavius depresses the clavicle and doesn't elevate the medial fragment.
C. Trapezius acts on the lateral fragment, and its failure to hold it up is what drops the shoulder.
D. Deltoid attaches laterally and doesn't move the medial fragment upward.
Objective: Identify the bony features of the clavicle, scapula, and humerus. Discuss common sites of fractures, predict what structures may be at risk, and discuss what sensory &/or motor deficits may occur.

Question 2037
During dissection of the shoulder, a tendon is traced to a small projection on the scapula located just superior to the glenoid cavity. Which of the following muscles most likely gives rise to that tendon?

The supraglenoid tubercle is the small projection superior to the glenoid cavity, and it's the origin of the long head of biceps brachii.
Why the other answers are wrong:

D. Supraspinatus arises from the supraspinous fossa on the posterior scapula.

Question 2038
During dissection of the posterior scapula, a muscle is found filling the smaller of the two fossae separated by the scapular spine, lying above that ridge. Which of the following muscles is most likely being examined?
A. Infraspinatus
B. Teres minor
C. Teres major

E. Subscapularis

The spine divides the posterior scapula into the supraspinous fossa, which is the smaller of the two and lies above the spine, and the larger infraspinous fossa below it. Supraspinatus attaches in the supraspinous fossa.
Why the other answers are wrong:

B. Teres minor attaches to the middle part of the lateral border of the scapula.
C. Teres major attaches at the inferior angle of the scapula.

Reference: Scapulothoracic interface; Sternoclavicular joint: type and articulation
Why this is correct:
Movement of the scapula at the scapulothoracic interface depends on movement at the sternoclavicular and acromioclavicular joints, so losing motion at the sternoclavicular joint limits how the scapula can move on the thorax.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Glenohumeral rotation depends on that joint's own capsule and muscles.
B. Forearm rotation occurs at the radioulnar joints.
C. Inferior translation at the glenohumeral joint depends on its capsule and cuff.
D. Elbow motion is unrelated to the sternoclavicular joint.
Objective: Describe the anatomical characteristics (osteology, ligaments, tendons, and capsule) of the sternoclavicular, acromioclavicular and glenohumeral joints. Discuss the functions of the joints, and distinguish the nerves that convey joint pain and proprioception following Hilton's Law.

Question 2092
A 72-year-old woman sustained a fracture of the proximal humerus. Six weeks later the rounded contour of that shoulder has disappeared, there's a slight hollow just below the acromion, and sensation over the point of the shoulder is reduced. Which of the following nerves is most likely injured?

Question 2115
During a motion analysis session, a subject abducts the upper limb through its full range. Which of the following best describes the division of that motion between the glenohumeral joint and the scapulothoracic interface?

B. 60 degrees at the glenohumeral joint and 120 degrees at the scapulothoracic interface
C. 180 degrees at the glenohumeral joint and no motion at the scapulothoracic interface
D. 90 degrees at the glenohumeral joint and 90 degrees at the scapulothoracic interface

Order: Second
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Scapulohumeral rhythm; Scapulothoracic interface

Scapulohumeral rhythm runs at a 2:1 ratio, so 120 degrees of glenohumeral motion plus 60 degrees of scapular rotation produces 180 degrees of total abduction.
Why the other answers are wrong:

D. An equal split would be a 1:1 ratio rather than the 2:1 rhythm described.

Question 2163
A 57-year-old woman with diabetes comes to the clinic because of several months of shoulder pain and progressive stiffness, and she now has difficulty abducting the arm. Passive and active range of motion are both reduced. Which of the following best explains her findings?
A. Fibrocartilaginous detachment of the glenoid labrum from the glenoid rim
B. Anterior displacement of the humeral head through a weak anteroinferior capsule
C. A tear of the supraspinatus tendon that disrupts the deltoid force couple
D. Adhesive fibrosis and scarring that thicken and tighten the joint capsule
E. Rupture of the coracoclavicular ligament with superior displacement of the clavicle

Order: Third
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Adhesive capsulitis; Fibrous capsule of the glenohumeral joint
Why this is correct:
Adhesive capsulitis, or frozen shoulder, occurs when adhesive fibrosis or scarring thickens and tightens the glenohumeral joint capsule, producing pain, stiffness, and difficulty abducting the arm. Diabetes is one of its risk factors.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Labral detachment is not the mechanism described for frozen shoulder in this lecture.
B. Anterior displacement of the head describes glenohumeral dislocation, which is an acute event.
C. A cuff tear limits active abduction but does not stiffen the joint in both active and passive motion.
E. Coracoclavicular rupture is an acromioclavicular dislocation presenting after trauma to the tip of the shoulder.
Objective: Discuss the clinical presentation and anatomical basis for the following: rotator cuff injuries, dislocation of the sternoclavicular joint, dislocation of the acromioclavicular joint (shoulder separation), dislocation of the glenohumeral joint (shoulder dislocation), and shoulder impingement/instability.

Answer: B. The cells have migrated from the dermis up through the epidermis into the scale
Order: Third
Difficulty: Hard
Reference: Munro microabscesses; Psoriasis histopathology
Why this is correct:
Neutrophils are blood-derived and reach the skin through dermal vessels, so finding them in the stratum corneum means they have travelled the full thickness of the epidermis to sit in the scale.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Keratinocytes do not produce neutrophils.
C. The lecture does not describe entry through follicular openings.
D. Munro microabscesses are collections of neutrophils rather than keratinocyte debris.
E. Sweat ducts are not described as a route in this lecture.

Question 2239
A higher power view of the same biopsy is shown in the attached image. Which of the following findings accounts for the marked hyperpigmentation seen as these lesions heal?
![H and E micrograph](library/images/msk-week-14/questions/q-papu-040.jpg)

B. Parakeratosis retaining melanin in the stratum corneum

Answer: C. Basal cell vacuolization with pigment incontinence
Order: Third
Difficulty: Hard
Reference: Lichen planus histology: interface dermatitis

Why this is correct:

![H and E micrograph](library/images/msk-week-14/questions/q-neo-137.jpg)
A. Epidermal inclusion cyst
B. Acrochordon
C. Seborrheic keratosis
D. Pilar cyst
E. Dermatofibroma
Answer: A. Epidermal inclusion cyst
Order: Second
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Epidermal inclusion cyst (follicular infundibular cyst); Hair follicle anatomy behind the follicular cysts
Why this is correct:
A granular layer in the lining with loose lamellar keratin identifies a cyst derived from the follicular infundibulum, which the lecture calls an epidermal inclusion cyst.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. An acrochordon is a polypoid outgrowth of normal skin, not a cyst.
C. A seborrheic keratosis contains keratin pseudocysts but is an exophytic epidermal plaque.
D. A pilar cyst lining has no granular layer and the keratin is dense.
E. A dermatofibroma is a solid spindle cell proliferation rather than a cyst.

B. Mesenchymal neoplasms arise from fat, fibrous tissue, nerve, vessel and muscle.
C. Merkel cell carcinoma is the neuroendocrine carcinoma and arises from Merkel cells in the basal layer.
D. Melanocytic neoplasms arise from melanocytes in the basal layer.
E. Epithelial and tumour-like lesions arise from the epidermis.

B. Most cases occur on the lower extremities and often recur
C. Most cases occur on the face and rarely recur
D. Most cases occur on the trunk and resolve without recurrence
E. Most cases occur in the axillae and groin and recur at puberty
Answer: B. Most cases occur on the lower extremities and often recur
Order: Second
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Erysipelas: presentation and predisposing conditions
Why this is correct:
The lecture gives the lower extremities as the site in 85 percent of cases and notes that erysipelas is often recurrent.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Water exposure points to *Aeromonas* or *Vibrio* infections.
C. Facial erysipelas is the uncommon presentation, and it's where rare *S. aureus* cases occur.
D. The trunk isn't given as a typical site.
E. The axillae and groin with onset at puberty describe hidradenitis suppurativa.

E. Sinus tracts are a late consequence of chronic inflammation.

A 60-year-old diabetic woman with rapidly progressive necrosis of the perineum is taken to the operating room, where the findings shown in the attached image are encountered. Which of the following best describes the operative principle the lecture applies here?
![Intraoperative photograph](library/images/msk-week-14/questions/q-ssti-045.jpg)
A. Conservative debridement with planned second look in one week
B. Emergency wide debridement
C. Incision and drainage of the fluctuant area only
D. Primary closure after irrigation
E. Debridement deferred until culture results return
Answer: B. Emergency wide debridement
Order: Second
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Necrotizing fasciitis type I: management
Why this is correct:
The lecture's management of type I necrotizing fasciitis is emergency wide debridement, because antibiotics can't reach necrotic tissue that has lost its blood supply.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Conservative debridement leaves necrotic tissue behind and allows progression.
C. Incision and drainage is the treatment for a furuncle or carbuncle.
D. Primary closure isn't appropriate over necrotic or contaminated tissue.
E. Waiting for cultures delays the only intervention that controls the infection.

Why the other answers are wrong:

Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Urticaria: wheals and the under 24 hour rule
Why this is correct:
The lecture defines urticaria as pruritic pink or pale flesh-colored wheals that are evanescent, with each lesion lasting less than 24 hours. The eruption as a whole continues because new wheals keep forming while old ones clear.
Why the other answers are wrong:

A 48-year-old woman is evaluated for recurrent pruritic swellings, each of which resolves within several hours. A punch biopsy is taken from an active lesion. Which of the following microscopic findings would be most consistent with the mechanism underlying her eruption?

Question 2759
A 52-year-old man cannot be diagnosed from his shoulder radiographs, which are normal, and the study shown in the attached image establishes the problem. Which of the following best explains why radiography could not answer the question?
![Diagnostic image](library/images/msk-week-14/questions/q-imag-047.jpg)
A. The rotator cuff is obscured by the acromion only in older patients
B. The rotator cuff is soft tissue, which plain films cannot image adequately
C. The rotator cuff is best assessed on weightbearing views
D. Radiography cannot be performed in patients with shoulder pain
E. Radiography shows the cuff but cannot show the humeral head
Answer: B. The rotator cuff is soft tissue, which plain films cannot image adequately
Order: Second
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Imaging suspected rotator cuff disease; Indications and contraindications for MRI
Why this is correct:
The study shown is an MRI, and the lecture assigns soft tissue derangement that plain films cannot image adequately to MRI, which is why the normal radiographs left the diagnosis open.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. The lecture does not make this an age dependent obscuration.
C. Weightbearing views are listed for the knee and ankle.
D. Radiography is in fact the first study obtained in this scenario.
E. Radiography shows the humeral head well, since it is bone.
Objective: Describe common indications for the use of each imaging modality.

MSK / Week 14 / Musculoskeletal Imaging Basics
Question 2760
A 30-year-old lacrosse player felt his shoulder slip out of place at a face off and go back in on its own, with tingling down the arm afterward. He reports several previous self-reduced dislocations. Radiographs have been obtained. Which of the following best explains why cross sectional imaging is obtained next?
A. Radiographs cannot show the humeral head
B. Radiographs cannot be obtained in recurrent dislocators
C. Cross sectional imaging replaces the need for a physical examination
D. The labrum, capsule and bony glenoid margins are not assessable on plain films
E. Cross sectional imaging is required before any reduction
Answer: D. The labrum, capsule and bony glenoid margins are not assessable on plain films
Order: Third
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Imaging recurrent shoulder dislocation; Normal MRI appearance of the shoulder
Why this is correct:
Recurrent instability damages the labrum and capsule along with the bony margins of the glenoid and humeral head, and those are cross sectional and soft tissue questions rather than plain film ones.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. The humeral head is bone and appears well on a radiograph.
B. Radiographs were obtained in this patient.
C. Imaging supplements rather than replaces examination in this lecture.
E. The shoulder in this scenario has already self-reduced.
Objective: Describe common indications for the use of each imaging modality.

MSK / Week 14 / Musculoskeletal Imaging Basics
Question 2761
A 30-year-old man reports tingling down the arm immediately after his shoulder dislocated and self-reduced. Which of the following structures is most likely responsible for that symptom?
A. The axillary nerve
B. The long thoracic nerve
C. The suprascapular nerve
D. The dorsal scapular nerve
E. The thoracodorsal nerve
Answer: A. The axillary nerve
Order: Third
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Imaging recurrent shoulder dislocation
Why this is correct:
The axillary nerve is the structure put at risk by a glenohumeral dislocation, which is why neurologic symptoms accompanying the injury point there.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. The long thoracic nerve is associated with serratus anterior and winged scapula.
C. The suprascapular nerve is associated with the suprascapular notch rather than dislocation.
D. The dorsal scapular nerve supplies the rhomboids and levator scapulae.
E. The thoracodorsal nerve supplies latissimus dorsi.
Objective: Briefly discuss imaging manifestations of common pathologies.

MSK / Week 14 / Musculoskeletal Imaging Basics
Question 2762
A physician evaluating a recurrent shoulder dislocator explains that plain films are still obtained first even though they will not answer the main question. Which of the following best supports obtaining them?
A. They establish the bony anatomy and exclude a fracture before further imaging
B. They are the definitive study for labral injury
C. They are required to assess the joint capsule
D. They substitute for examination of the axillary nerve
E. They are the only study that can be obtained after reduction
Answer: A. They establish the bony anatomy and exclude a fracture before further imaging
Order: Second
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Imaging recurrent shoulder dislocation; When to order a radiograph
Why this is correct:
Radiographs are the lecture's study for fractures, and across every clinical scenario in the deck the plain film comes first to answer the bony question before cross sectional imaging addresses soft tissue.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Labral injury is assessed on cross sectional imaging.
C. The capsule is soft tissue and is not assessed on plain films.
D. Imaging does not substitute for neurologic examination.
E. Cross sectional imaging can also be obtained after reduction.
Objective: Describe common indications for the use of each imaging modality.

MSK / Week 14 / Musculoskeletal Imaging Basics
Question 2763
A 20-year-old collegiate distance runner has two months of worsening right anterior shin pain during runs, now present on long walks between classes, worse with running and better with rest. The study shown in the attached image is obtained. Which of the following best identifies it?
![Diagnostic image](library/images/msk-week-14/questions/q-imag-049.jpg)
A. Axial computed tomography of the lower leg
B. Frontal radiograph of the lower leg
C. Mortise view of the ankle
D. Sunrise view of the knee
E. Cross sectional magnetic resonance image of the lower leg
Answer: E. Cross sectional magnetic resonance image of the lower leg
Order: Second
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Stress reactions and their imaging; T1 versus T2 weighted MRI
Why this is correct:
The image is a cross sectional slice through the leg in which cortical bone is dark and the soft tissues are differentiated in greyscale, which is the MRI appearance rather than that of a radiograph or CT.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. On CT bone appears bright and sharply defined rather than dark.
B. A radiograph is a superimposed projection in which bone is bright white.
C. The mortise view is an ankle projection.
D. The sunrise view is a knee projection showing the patella end on.
Objective: Establish familiarity with imaging appearance of basic anatomical structures.

MSK / Week 14 / Musculoskeletal Imaging Basics
Question 2764
A 20-year-old runner has two months of worsening anterior shin pain, worse with running and better with rest, and the study shown in the attached image is obtained. Which of the following best describes the bone process underlying this appearance?
![Magnetic resonance image](library/images/msk-week-14/questions/q-imag-050.jpg)
A. Bone resorption stops entirely, leaving brittle cortex
B. A tendon progressively pulls a fragment from its attachment
C. Bone is crushed down on itself by repeated loading
D. Osteoclastic activity exceeds osteoblastic activity, leaving weakened bone
E. Osteoblastic activity exceeds osteoclastic activity, producing dense new bone
Answer: D. Osteoclastic activity exceeds osteoblastic activity, leaving weakened bone
Order: Third
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Stress reactions and their imaging; T1 versus T2 weighted MRI
Why this is correct:
The lecture states that bone under stress normally responds with osteoblastic activity laying down new bone, but that in a stress reaction osteoclastic activity occurs at a greater rate than osteoblastic activity, leaving weakened bone that progresses toward fracture without intervention.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Resorption continues and in fact outpaces formation.
B. Progressive tendon traction describes an avulsion.
C. Crushing describes a compression fracture.
E. That describes the normal adaptive response rather than a stress reaction.
Objective: Briefly discuss imaging manifestations of common pathologies.

Question 2765
A 20-year-old runner with anterior shin pain has normal plain films of the tibia, and the study shown in the attached image is obtained next. Which of the following best explains why this study was chosen?
![Magnetic resonance image](library/images/msk-week-14/questions/q-imag-049.jpg)
A. It measures bone density more accurately than radiography
B. It replaces the need to modify the patient's training
C. It categorizes the extent of the reaction and detects it before fracture occurs
D. It is the only study that shows the tibial cortex
E. It is required before any plain film can be repeated
Answer: C. It categorizes the extent of the reaction and detects it before fracture occurs
Order: Third
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Stress reactions and their imaging; Indications and contraindications for MRI
Why this is correct:
The lecture says initial imaging is plain films to evaluate for fracture, and that the best imaging is MRI because it best categorizes the extent of the stress reaction and will pick up reactions that have not yet resulted in fracture.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Bone density assessment is part of the radiographic survey in this lecture.
B. Imaging does not substitute for intervention, which the lecture says is needed to prevent progression.
D. The cortex is well shown on plain radiographs.
E. The lecture does not make MRI a prerequisite for repeat radiography.
Objective: Describe common indications for the use of each imaging modality.

Question 2766
A 30-year-old lacrosse player has had several shoulder dislocations, and his imaging shows the two bony lesions the lecture labels on its radiograph. Which of the following structures does the Hill-Sachs defect involve?
A. The coracoid process
B. The glenoid rim
C. The acromion
D. The humeral head
E. The clavicle
Answer: D. The humeral head
Order: First
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Hill-Sachs and Bankart lesions after shoulder dislocation; Imaging recurrent shoulder dislocation
Why this is correct:
On the deck's radiograph the Hill-Sachs label and its arrow point at the humeral head, at its upper outer margin, while the Bankart label points at the glenoid.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. The coracoid process is a normal landmark on the shoulder film.
B. The glenoid rim is where the slide's Bankart arrow points.
C. The acromion is labeled on the lecture's normal shoulder film rather than marked as a lesion here.
E. The clavicle is a normal landmark on the shoulder film.
Objective: Briefly discuss imaging manifestations of common pathologies.

Question 2767
A patient with recurrent anterior shoulder instability is found to have a bony defect of the socket side of the joint, which the lecture marks with a boxed label on its radiograph. Which of the following names that lesion?
A. Calcific tendinopathy
B. Hill-Sachs lesion
C. Rotator cuff tear
D. Acromioclavicular separation
E. Bankart lesion
Answer: E. Bankart lesion
Order: Second
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Hill-Sachs and Bankart lesions after shoulder dislocation; Imaging recurrent shoulder dislocation
Why this is correct:
The socket of the glenohumeral joint is the glenoid, and on the deck's radiograph the Bankart label and its arrow point at the glenoid rim.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Calcific tendinopathy is one of the three indications the lecture gives for plain radiography.
B. The Hill-Sachs label on the same film points at the humeral head, which is the ball rather than the socket.
C. A rotator cuff tear is the soft tissue injury in the lecture's separate overhead pain scenario.
D. An acromioclavicular separation involves the joint between the clavicle and the acromion.
Objective: Briefly discuss imaging manifestations of common pathologies.

Question 2768
A 30-year-old man with recurrent shoulder dislocations has already had plain films, and the study shown in the attached image is obtained next. Which of the following best explains why this study was chosen?
![Diagnostic image](library/images/msk-week-14/questions/q-imag-057.jpg)
A. It is the first-line study after any dislocation
B. It shows the rotator cuff tendons in fine detail
C. It can be obtained with the patient weightbearing
D. It shows the glenoid and the humeral head in cross section
E. It measures the acromioclavicular distance directly
Answer: D. It shows the glenoid and the humeral head in cross section
Order: Third
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Hill-Sachs and Bankart lesions after shoulder dislocation; How CT produces an image and when to order it
Why this is correct:
The study is a CT, which the lecture chooses when bone needs to be seen in cross section, and the bony surfaces damaged by recurrent instability are the humeral head and the glenoid rim.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. The lecture obtains plain radiographs first in this patient.
B. Fine soft tissue detail is what the lecture assigns to MRI rather than CT.
C. Weightbearing is a plain film technique listed for the knee and ankle.
E. The acromioclavicular distance is measured on the plain film.
Objective: Describe common indications for the use of each imaging modality.

Question 2769
A 23-year-old man felt a pop in his knee while planting his leg and has a persistent effusion. The lecture's own magnetic resonance image for this scenario carries a caption naming what it shows. Which of the following does that image demonstrate?
A. A normal study
B. An occult tibial plateau fracture
C. A torn medial meniscus
D. An absent anterior cruciate ligament
E. A ruptured patellar ligament
Answer: D. An absent anterior cruciate ligament
Order: Second
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Imaging an acute knee injury with a pop and effusion; Normal MRI appearance of the knee
Why this is correct:
The sagittal image the lecture shows for this patient is captioned NO ACL, with an ellipse drawn around the intercondylar notch where the ligament should run, so the study confirms the tear.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. The caption identifies a missing structure rather than a normal study.
B. A tibial plateau fracture would be a bony finding, and the radiograph in this scenario showed no fracture.
C. The lecture's caption names the cruciate rather than a meniscus.
E. The patellar ligament is not the structure the lecture marks on this image.
Objective: Briefly discuss imaging manifestations of common pathologies.

Question 2770
A 23-year-old man who felt a pop in his knee five days ago, with swelling that has persisted, has the study shown in the attached image as his first investigation. Which of the following does this study most directly rule out?
![Radiograph](library/images/msk-week-14/questions/q-imag-042.jpg)
A. A fracture
B. A meniscal tear
C. A capsular injury
D. A cruciate ligament tear
E. An articular cartilage tear
Answer: A. A fracture
Order: Third
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Imaging an acute knee injury with a pop and effusion; When to order a radiograph
Why this is correct:
Fractures are the first of the three indications the lecture gives for plain radiography, and in this scenario the film is obtained to exclude a fracture before the soft tissue question is addressed on MRI.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. A meniscus is soft tissue and is evaluated on MRI.
C. The joint capsule is soft tissue and is not assessed on a plain film.
D. A cruciate ligament is soft tissue and is evaluated on MRI.
E. Articular cartilage is not evaluated directly on a plain radiograph in this lecture.
Objective: Describe common indications for the use of each imaging modality.

Question 2771
A 48-year-old woman splinted two weeks earlier for snuffbox tenderness returns for repeat imaging, and the study shown in the attached image is obtained. An arrow marks the bone of interest. Which of the following carpal bones is indicated?
![Diagnostic image](library/images/msk-week-14/questions/q-imag-059.jpg)
A. Scaphoid
B. Triquetrum
C. Hamate
D. Capitate
E. Lunate
Answer: A. Scaphoid
Order: Third
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Imaging a suspected scaphoid fracture and occult fracture follow-up; Normal wrist and carpal anatomy on imaging
Why this is correct:
The arrow points at the bone on the radial side of the proximal carpal row, sitting directly against the distal radius, which is the scaphoid, and it is the bone the lecture's fall on an outstretched hand scenario turns on.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. The triquetrum sits at the ulnar end of the proximal row.
C. The hamate sits in the distal row on the ulnar side.
D. The capitate sits in the distal row in the centre of the carpus.
E. The lunate sits in the proximal row on the ulnar side of the scaphoid.
Objective: Establish familiarity with imaging appearance of basic anatomical structures.

Question 2773
The cross sectional study shown in the attached image was obtained to assess bone detail after an injury. Which of the following regions does it show?
![Diagnostic image](library/images/msk-week-14/questions/q-imag-060.jpg)
A. Shoulder
B. Knee
C. Elbow
D. Wrist
E. Ankle
Answer: D. Wrist
Order: Second
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: CT appearance of the shoulder, knee and wrist; Normal wrist and carpal anatomy on imaging
Why this is correct:
The slice shows two rows of small rounded carpal bones packed between the end of a forearm bone and the bases of the metacarpals, which is the carpus.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. The shoulder would show the humeral head against the glenoid with the scapula behind it.
B. The knee would show the femoral condyles against the tibial plateau.
C. The elbow would show the distal humerus against the radius and ulna.
E. The ankle would show the talus beneath the tibial plafond.
Objective: Establish familiarity with imaging appearance of basic anatomical structures.
